common_name: Dixie Speckled Butterpea (Red-Speckled Southern Bush Lima)

planting.note: Direct sow an inch deep once soil is reliably warm past 65F, since this bush-type sieva lima rots quickly in cool, damp spring ground.

directions: Direct sow into warm, light, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants close in rows about two feet apart since this variety stays compact and needs no support. This old Southern bush butterpea produces heavily branched plants that keep flowering and setting pods through the hottest, driest stretches of summer when many bean types shut down. Pods run about four inches long and typically hold three or four small, rounded seeds boldly mottled maroon-on-pink, a color pattern that sets it apart from plain cream-seeded butterpea types. Pick at the green-shell stage for classic buttery flavor, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage and seed saving.
sources: Southern heirloom seed retailers (Thresh Seed Co., Mary's Heirloom Seeds, Harvesting History)

common_name: Hickory Cane Dent Corn (Pre-1875 Florida/Georgia Heirloom Field Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least four short rows after frost danger has passed, for reliable wind pollination of this very tall heirloom dent corn.

directions: Sow in blocks rather than single rows for good pollination, in fertile soil with steady moisture through tasseling and ear fill, since stalks of this variety can tower up to 15 feet. Hickory Cane predates 1875 and traces to corn grown in north Florida and south Georgia before spreading north through the Southern Appalachians as a staple grain corn. Plants typically carry one to two ears with large white kernels, and tightly wrapped husks help shield developing ears from weevils and earworms in the field. Left to dry fully on the stalk, the grain grinds into classic coarse white cornmeal and grits, and also makes excellent hominy.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills spaced widely apart after soil has thoroughly warmed, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room to ramble.

directions: Plant in deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun, watering consistently through fruit set and tapering off as melons approach ripeness to build sugar. Reuben Kolb of Alabama developed this variety around 1885, and its unusually tough, bruise-resistant rind made it one of the first watermelons durable enough for long-distance rail shipping, briefly making it a dominant commercial melon of the late 19th century before later shipping varieties displaced it. Fruits are large and nearly round, often reaching 50 pounds or more under good growing conditions, with sweet, deep red flesh prized for home and market eating. Because the rind is tougher than modern melon-market types, it also stores and travels unusually well for a home garden heirloom.

common_name: Old Timey Green Collard (North Carolina Heirloom Non-Heading Collard)

planting.note: Start indoors or direct sow 10-14 weeks before first fall frost; in zone 9, set out transplants in late summer for a fall-through-winter harvest that sweetens after frost.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously since this heirloom spreads wide and low rather than growing into a tall, upright stalk collard. Old Timey Green is a rare non-heading North Carolina family strain, saved for decades before passing into seed-bank preservation efforts, and it remains scarce in cultivation today, distinct from the separately preserved Old Timey Blue strain. Leaves are broadly elliptic with a wavy edge and only light blistering, often carrying purple tinting at the stem and leaf base, and cook up with a notably strong, earthy flavor and a bit more bitterness than milder modern collard hybrids. Harvest outer leaves continually through the cool season, and consider saving seed from vigorous plants to help keep this dwindling family heirloom in circulation.
